performers: The Griller String Quartet: Sidney Griller and Jack O’Brien, violins; Philip Burton, viola; Colin Hampton, cello
intro: After serious illness in 1825, Beethoven writes a “holy song of thanksgiving” for four string players. The Griller Quartet plays its long hymn and the two D-major passages where he writes that he feels new strength.

sections.label: A · A hymn on the white notes
sections.mNote: F Lydian; short imitations open into long chords

sections.label: B · Feeling new strength
sections.mNote: D-major Andante in 3/8, with trills and quick violin runs

sections.label: A′ · The hymn returns with moving companions
sections.mNote: Long violin notes above more active lower strings

sections.label: B′ · The D-major dance returns
sections.mNote: The violin decorates the tune with quicker notes

sections.label: A″ · With the deepest feeling
sections.mNote: The final hymn passes its phrases through all four parts

cues.title: Four players begin a hymn
cues.text: A short phrase passes from the first violin down through the quartet. Then the players settle into long, hymn-like chords. Beethoven calls this music a “holy song of thanksgiving of a convalescent to the Deity, in the Lydian mode”.
cues.evidence: Beethoven’s heading in Op. 132, III, 1825; our translation. Breitkopf & Härtel, Werke, Serie 6 No. 51, 1863, printed p. 173. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Opus132.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The hymn’s B natural
cues.text: The hymn rests on F, but its scale has B♮ where F major has B♭. That extra half-step opens a wide space above the home note. Beethoven’s Lydian mode uses the seven white notes of a keyboard, with F at their centre.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 173: Beethoven’s Lydian heading, no key signature, F-centred harmony and B♮.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: A spring spent ill
cues.text: In the spring of 1825, serious illness interrupts Beethoven’s work on this quartet. He returns to it during his recovery and completes it in July. His own words above the slow movement make the thanksgiving personal.
cues.evidence: Beethoven-Haus, Beethoven’s String Quartets exhibition guide, pp. 7–8: illness in spring 1825 and completion in July. https://internet.beethoven.de/pdf-sonderausstellung/Beethovens-Streichquartette-Brief-Guide.pdf

cues.title: Feeling new strength
cues.text: The strings step into D major and a quicker three-beat gait. A first-violin trill gives way to little runs; the cello lifts the tune with short upward figures. Beethoven writes Neue Kraft fühlend — feeling new strength.
cues.evidence: Beethoven’s inscription at the first Andante, Op. 132, III, 1825; our translation. Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 173–174: D major, 3/8, violin trill and rising cello figures.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The hymn has companions
cues.text: The slow hymn returns, with longer notes in the first violin and moving lines below. The other players curl around the melody, sometimes answering it, sometimes carrying on while it holds a note. F and its natural-note scale are home again.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 175, Molto adagio: cancelled key signature, common time, sustained first violin and altered lower parts.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A copyist gets a headache
cues.text: Before the quartet can be played, its parts need copying. Cellist Joseph Linke tackles the manuscript, but the effort gives him a headache. Violinist Karl Holz takes over the last movement. Beethoven checks and corrects the parts himself.
cues.evidence: Holz’s entry in Beethoven’s conversation book, about 13 August 1825, BKh 8 p. 39, transcribed at https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus132/; Beethoven-Haus guide, pp. 7–8, describes copying and corrections.

cues.title: The violin adds flourishes
cues.text: D major and the Andante return. The first violin dresses the tune in runs and trills, while the lower strings keep its springing accompaniment. The change from long hymn notes to these small, nimble figures feels almost physical.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 175–177, second Andante: D major, 3/8, ornamented violin line and accompanying figures.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: With the deepest feeling
cues.text: Mit innigster Empfindung — with the deepest feeling — appears beside each player’s returning phrase. The final hymn begins with one voice answering another. Its long notes and curling figures pass among all four instruments; there is no further dance.
cues.evidence: Beethoven’s instructions at the final Molto adagio, Op. 132, III, 1825; our translation. Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 178–179: successive inscribed entries and final slow span.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fourteen guests at an inn
cues.text: On 9 September 1825, fourteen invited guests hear the quartet at Vienna’s Zum Wilden Mann inn. Two days later it is played again, with the visiting British musician George Smart among the listeners.
cues.evidence: Private hearings of 9 and 11 September 1825, location, guest count and Smart’s attendance: https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus132/.

cues.title: The last F chord
cues.text: The hymn approaches its final F-major chord. Moving phrases give way to held notes, and Beethoven asks for pianissimo. The first violin rests high above the cello’s F; all four players hold the ending under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 179, end of III: F-major chord, pp and fermatas. The cue retains the established closing passage time.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: F gives way to D major
transitions.from: A · A hymn on the white notes
transitions.how: The hymn closes on F, with the first violin holding its upper note under a fermata. Neue Kraft fühlend introduces a D-major Andante in 3/8. F♯ and C♯ enter the signature; the first violin trills while the cello starts a short rising figure. Long chords give way to a buoyant dance.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel, Werke, Serie 6 No. 51, printed p. 173. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Opus132.pdf

transitions.title: The sharps disappear from the page
transitions.to: A′ · The hymn returns with moving companions
transitions.how: The Andante’s violin figures grow quieter above a descending cello line. Beethoven cancels the two-sharp signature and restores common time at Molto adagio. The F-Lydian hymn returns in long first-violin notes, with the lower strings moving more freely beneath it.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 175, first system and following hymn. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Opus132.pdf

transitions.title: The dance comes back decorated
transitions.from: A′ · The hymn returns with moving companions
transitions.how: The second hymn closes over F in the cello. The bass moves to D, and the two-sharp signature and 3/8 return with Andante. The first violin leaps into the upper register; its tune now carries quicker flourishes above the lower strings’ rising accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 175–176, second Andante. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Opus132.pdf

transitions.title: One voice answers another
transitions.how: The second Andante subsides, and Molto adagio restores common time and F Lydian. Second violin, viola and cello enter in turn before the first violin joins their moving phrases. Beethoven writes Mit innigster Empfindung beside each entry. The hymn’s long notes gradually emerge among those lines.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 178, final Molto adagio and its inscribed entries. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Opus132.pdf

source.title: Beethoven, Op.132 — Breitkopf & Härtel, Beethovens Werke, 1863, plate B.51
source.locator: Printed pp. 173–179, movement III. Two violins, viola and cello, with one player on each part.

timeline.note: The players enter one by one, then settle into long hymn chords.
The first violin trills and runs above short rising figures in the lower strings.
Long first-violin notes carry the hymn above moving phrases in the other three parts.
The returning D-major tune gains quicker flourishes in the first violin.
Each player takes up the final hymn’s curling phrases; long violin notes rise above them towards the quiet F-major close.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Original quartet scoring; movement III. The Archive’s combined III–IV designation is disputed.
fields.note: The exact selected 1092.62-second MP3 is retained without truncation or substitution. Its analysed structure supports the five alternating spans of III, at approximately 0, 214, 340, 558 and 686 seconds, followed by slow music through the endpoint. The required report does not establish an A-major march or the IV–V link. Supplementary upper-band inspection finds an F-centred ending; verifier VerH independently checked the selected file’s final37.6s against the score and also found the F ending of III, not IV’s dominant recitative. These are score/audio-feature correspondences, not an aural or complete bar-aligned certification. No IV boundary or IV listening prose is invented. Performing edition, cuts, repeat observance and the completeness of the final played release remain unestablished.
alts: III–IV combined, as asserted by the Archive filename and catalogue metadata
III only, supported by the selected file’s five-span design and independently checked F-centred endpoint

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition and the nineteenth-century Breitkopf & Härtel quartet score are public domain.
fields.note: The quartet was composed in 1825; Beethoven died in 1827. The consulted Beethovens Werke engraving, plate B.51, is catalogued as the 1863 edition and Public Domain. This does not clear an unidentified later performing edition or the sleeve author’s prose.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU public-domain basis only: the recording was published before 1963; US status is not established.
fields.note: The admitted basis is eu-published-before-1963, using the Archive’s 1952 catalogue date for this identified London LLP318 issue. The printed sleeve carries a 1951 copyright notice, corroborating an early-1950s package but not independently establishing the first publication year of the sound recording. A recording published by 1952 had exhausted the ordinary EU 50-year phonogram term before 1 November 2013; the 2011 extension applies to recordings still protected on that date. This is territorial, not a Creative Commons grant or worldwide clearance. The US 1947–1956 term is longer, and no US public-domain claim is made. The Archive item supplies no separate recording licence; availability online and Beethoven’s public-domain composition are not the admission basis.

composer.epithet: He could make a symphony out of four notes, and spent his last years finding things four string players had never said.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. Music was the family trade. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, learning operas from the middle of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was supposed to come back. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him disappeared.
